title: A close reading of BERT: how fill-in-the-blank training teaches language understanding
summary: BERT has a Transformer encoder fill in blanks over 3.3 billion words of text, then attaches a single output layer that handles classification, QA, and tagging—setting records on 11 tasks at once. We unpack its two pretraining tasks, input format, and fine-tuning recipe, using worked examples and ablation results to show why it works and what it leaves unsolved.
ai_summary: BERT (Google AI Language, 2018) pretrains a Transformer encoder bidirectionally: it masks 15% of tokens at random and asks the model to predict them (80% [MASK], 10% random tokens, 10% unchanged), while also predicting whether two sentences are consecutive. Pretraining uses BooksCorpus plus English Wikipedia, 3.3 billion words total; BASE (110M parameters) and LARGE (340M parameters) each train for 4 days. At fine-tuning time, a single output layer is added and the model sets records on 11 tasks: GLUE 80.5 (up 7.7 points), SQuAD v1.1 test F1 93.2, SQuAD v2.0 83.1. Ablations show most of the gain comes from bidirectionality; limits include [MASK] appearing only during pretraining, only 15% of tokens predicted per batch, a 512-token maximum input length, and weak generation.
brief: Problem: earlier pretrained models (GPT, ELMo) are all unidirectional, so each token's representation lacks context from the other side—especially costly for tasks like question answering.
Method: mask 15% of tokens and have the model predict them bidirectionally; add a next-sentence prediction task; pack every input into one sequence with [CLS] and [SEP].
Result: with only one layer added at fine-tuning, it sets records on 11 tasks—GLUE up 7.7 points, SQuAD v2.0 up 5.1 points.
Takeaway: at equal size, bidirectional beats unidirectional; larger models help even small tasks with only a few thousand examples.

paper.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
paper.authors: Jacob Devlin, Ming-Wei Chang, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova

cover.headline: A close reading of the BERT paper
cover.highlight: Fill-in-the-blank teaches machines to read language

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In October 2018, four Google AI Language researchers released **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers). Its recipe has two steps: first, a Transformer encoder repeatedly does fill-in-the-blank over 3.3 billion words of books and Wikipedia text to learn language itself; then a small output layer is attached and lightly trained on a modest amount of task-specific labeled data.

That simple recipe set records on 11 natural language processing tasks: it pushed the GLUE score to 80.5, an immediate jump of 7.7 points; on reading comprehension, SQuAD v1.1 test F1 reached 93.2 and v2.0 reached 83.1, 5.1 points ahead of the previous best system. More importantly, where earlier tasks each required a purpose-built architecture, BERT was the first to show that **a single pretrained model plus one layer can handle them all**.

If the Transformer we read last time is the "engine" of large models, BERT is the paper that first proved the full recipe—pretrain on massive unlabeled text, then fine-tune for the task—actually works end to end. Today nearly every large model follows the same two-stage pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern; the mainstream later just switched to the decoder-only GPT line.

callout.title: One-sentence version
callout.text: BERT = the Transformer encoder (every token attends to both left and right) + two pretraining tasks (mask 15% of tokens and predict them; decide whether two sentences are consecutive) + one uniform way to use it (one model, with a different input format and one output layer, can do classification, QA, and tagging).

callout.title: Four concepts for reading this paper
callout.text: If these are new to you, these four will do:
list: **Transformer encoder**: the part of the architecture that uses self-attention to let each token see the whole sentence. See our previous close reading of "Attention Is All You Need."
**Language model**: a model that predicts the next word from the words before it. GPT is trained this way.

**Pretraining and fine-tuning**: first learn general language knowledge from vast unlabeled text (like reading widely), then tune on a small amount of task-specific labeled data (like cramming before a test).
**Labeled data**: data with human-provided answers, such as "Is this movie review positive or negative?" It is expensive and scarce, while unlabeled text is almost unlimited.

sections.h: Before BERT: two approaches, one shared weakness

blocks.p: By 2018, there were already two main ways to apply pretrained models to downstream tasks, and the paper sets them out at the start:

list: **Feature-based**, represented by ELMo: pretrain a language model, then feed its word vectors into each task's purpose-built model as additional features. The pretrained model itself stays fixed.

**Fine-tuning-based**, represented by OpenAI's GPT: pretrain a Transformer language model, add only a small number of new parameters for each downstream task, and then retrain the entire model together with those new parameters.

blocks.p: The paper argues both share one weakness: **pretraining uses a unidirectional language model**. GPT reads left to right, so in self-attention each token sees only the words to its left. ELMo trains one left-to-right and one right-to-left model, but they are trained independently and simply concatenated at the end; inside the model, left and right context never really fuses.

callout.title: Why one direction hurts: an example
callout.text: Take "My new apple is delicious" and "My new apple is easy to use." By the time the model reaches "apple," the clue that tells it whether this is the fruit or an Apple phone lies to the **right** ("delicious" vs. "easy to use"). A left-to-right model at that position cannot see the following words at all; it can only wait. But many language-understanding tasks—such as finding where an answer starts in QA—require every position to know both sides at once.

fig.title: Three pretraining approaches compared: only BERT attends to both sides at every layer
fig.subtitle: Based on paper section 2 and appendix A.4. The amber row is BERT.
rows: Left and right trained separately, then concatenated

quiz.q: In the sentence "My new apple is easy to use," what information is available to a left-to-right language model when it processes the word "apple"?
options: The whole sentence
Only "my," "new," and "apple" itself
Only "easy to use"
Only "apple" itself
quiz.why: A left-to-right model can see only itself and the words to its left at each position. "Easy to use" is on the right, so it is not visible when processing "apple"; the model cannot decide at that point that this is an Apple phone. This is exactly why the paper says unidirectional models are weaker for tasks that need both sides of context.

sections.h: Why not just go bidirectional: the model would "see itself"

blocks.p: If bidirectional is better, why not simply train a bidirectional language model? The paper gives a key explanation: standard language models can only be trained unidirectionally, because with bidirectional conditioning **every word indirectly "sees itself,"** and the model could predict the target word trivially.

How exactly? Suppose the model must predict the 5th token. In layer 1, positions 4 and 6 both attend to token 5 via self-attention; in layer 2, when position 5 attends to positions 4 and 6, it is effectively receiving its own answer back. With enough layers, the answer leaks back from every direction, and the model learns only to copy answers rather than understand language.

callout.title: It is as if the answer were printed next to the exam question.
callout.text: A left-to-right language model is safe because, when predicting token 5, no position can see token 5 or anything after it. Once you allow bidirectionality without making any other change, the answer gets mixed into the question.

blocks.p: BERT's solution is simple: **if the word to be predicted will leak, mask it first.** That is the first pretraining task.

sections.h: Task 1: mask words and predict them—fill in the blanks

blocks.p: The paper calls this **Masked LM** (MLM) and notes that in the literature it is usually called a cloze task (proposed as early as 1953 to measure reading difficulty). The approach: randomly pick 15% of the tokens in a sequence, mask them, and have the model predict each original word from all remaining words—both left and right. The final-layer output at each masked position goes through a softmax over the whole vocabulary to score how likely the correct word is.

callout.title: What are "word pieces"?
callout.text: BERT does not process English as whole words; it uses WordPiece to split words into smaller pieces, with a 30,000-token vocabulary. Common words stay whole, while rare words are split—for example, the paper's diagram splits playing into play and ##ing (## means "attached to the previous piece"). Masking is done at the token level and does not try to respect whole words.

blocks.p: But this creates a new problem: during fine-tuning, [MASK] never appears in the input, so pretraining and fine-tuning don't match. The paper's fix is not to replace the selected 15% of positions all with [MASK]; instead it splits them 80/10/10 into three treatments. Its example is "my dog is hairy," and suppose hairy is selected:

fig.title: For each selected word: masked 80%, random 10%, unchanged 10%
fig.subtitle: Example from paper Appendix A.1; regardless of treatment, the model must predict the original word hairy at that position. The blue column shows what the model actually sees.
rows: Main case: force the model to predict from context
Prevents the model from trusting the visible word

plain.title: One blank, three ways of testing it
plain.text: The word chosen for prediction (here hairy) is usually replaced by [MASK]; sometimes by a random word (apple); and sometimes left exactly as is. The model never knows whether the word in front of it has been tampered with, so it must do real context-aware understanding at every position.

blocks.p: The elegance of this design is that the model never knows which positions will be tested or which words have been swapped, so it must **keep a good context-aware representation at every position**, not only when it sees [MASK]. Random replacements account for just 1.5% of all tokens (10% × 15%), which the paper argues does not hurt language understanding.

fig.title: Masking variants: fine-tuning tolerates them, but [MASK]-only clearly hurts feature-based use
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 8, dev set results. The first row is the scheme BERT uses; the amber row is "[MASK]-only."
fig.note: MNLI is sentence-relationship prediction (accuracy); NER is named entity recognition (F1). In the feature-based setting, model parameters are frozen and only features are extracted, so the pretrain–fine-tune mismatch cannot be repaired by fine-tuning—which is why the [MASK]-only problem is amplified.

blocks.p: There is another cost: a normal language model practices prediction at every position, while MLM predicts only 15% of tokens in each batch, so it learns somewhat slowly. The appendix compares this directly: MLM converges slightly slower than a left-to-right model, but its accuracy is higher almost from the beginning.

quiz.q: In a training input of 512 tokens, roughly how many positions are selected for prediction under BERT's rules, and about how many of them are replaced with random words?
options: 512 predicted positions, 51 random words
About 77 predicted positions, about 8 random ones
About 77 predicted positions, about 61 random ones
About 15 predicted positions, about 1 random one
quiz.why: 512 × 15% ≈ 77 positions are selected for prediction. Of those, 10% become random words—77 × 10% ≈ 8, or about 1.5% of all tokens. The rest divide into roughly 61 [MASK] replacements (80%) and about 8 unchanged.

quiz.q: Why not replace all 15% selected positions with [MASK]?
options: It would be too expensive computationally
Fine-tuning inputs contain no [MASK], so replacing all selected positions with [MASK] would create a mismatch; the mixed treatment also forces the model to represent every word properly
[MASK] would let the model see itself
The paper limits each sentence to one [MASK]
quiz.why: The paper says explicitly that this is to reduce the pretrain–fine-tune mismatch. The appendix goes further: because the model doesn't know which words will be tested or which have been swapped, it must keep a good contextual representation at every position. Table 8 also shows that [MASK]-only drops the most in the feature-based setting.

blocks.p: Many important tasks—question answering (the relationship between question and passage) and natural language inference (whether sentence B follows from sentence A)—require understanding **relationships between two sentences**, while masked-word prediction only exercises within-sentence structure. So the paper adds a second pretraining task: **Next Sentence Prediction** (NSP).

The method is just as simple and can be generated for free from any corpus: each training example is built from sentence A and sentence B; 50% of the time B is the actual next sentence after A (labeled IsNext), and 50% of the time B is a random sentence from the corpus (labeled NotNext). Two examples from the appendix:

fig.title: Next-sentence prediction: one true continuation, one random sentence
fig.subtitle: From paper Appendix A.1; both examples also include masking.

plain.title: Are these two sentences consecutive?
plain.text: Half the time the model sees a real adjacency, half the time the second sentence is drawn randomly from elsewhere, and the model must decide whether it is the actual next sentence. The goal is to teach BERT to look at relationships between sentences—though later work found this exercise matters less than originally thought.

blocks.p: The paper reports that the final model reaches 97%–98% accuracy on NSP. Ablations (detailed later) show that removing NSP clearly hurts question answering and sentence-inference tasks.

quiz.q: In NSP training data, true continuations and random sentences are each 50%. If a model learns nothing and always answers IsNext, what accuracy would it get? What does that suggest about the 97%–98% figure?
options: 0%, so 97% is extremely hard
50%; since random sentences often come from completely different topics, the task may be easier than it looks
100%, because most sentences are true continuations
Impossible to compute
quiz.why: Always guessing IsNext would be exactly 50% correct. More important: NotNext sentences are drawn at random and often discuss a completely different topic from A—say a store and penguins—so a model can answer most cases by checking whether topics are coherent, without truly understanding inter-sentence logic. Later work attacked NSP precisely from this angle.

callout.title: The later fate of NSP
callout.text: The paper's ablations support NSP. But later work—for example RoBERTa in 2019—found that with larger-scale training, dropping NSP does no harm; one likely reason is the issue above: randomly drawn sentences are too easy to distinguish. When reading papers, remember that an ablation conclusion holds under that paper's own settings.

sections.h: How inputs are assembled: one sequence for one or two sentences

blocks.p: To let one model handle many tasks, BERT packs all input into a single sequence: a special **[CLS]** token at the start, and **[SEP]** separators between two sentences and at the end. Here a "sentence" need not be a grammatical sentence; it can be any contiguous span of text. The whole sequence is at most 512 tokens.

The input vector at each position is the **sum** of three vectors: the token embedding, a "segment embedding" indicating whether the token belongs to sentence A or B, and a position embedding indicating its position. Unlike the original Transformer, which uses sinusoidal position encodings, BERT learns both its position embeddings and segment embeddings.

fig.title: Input vector = token embedding + segment embedding + position embedding
fig.subtitle: Redrawn from Figure 2 of the paper (first 7 positions shown). E is a learned vector; the subscript indicates what it corresponds to.
fig.note: The full example is [CLS] my dog is cute [SEP] he likes play ##ing [SEP] — 11 positions in total. All segment embeddings in the second sentence are E_{B}.

plain.title: Three transparent sheets stacked together
plain.text: Each position's input is built by stacking three sheets: the first says which word it is, the second says whether it belongs to sentence A or sentence B, and the third says which position it occupies. Add the three together, and one vector carries all three kinds of information.

blocks.p: The final-layer output for [CLS] (denoted C in the paper) serves as the summary of the whole sequence and is used for classification tasks and NSP; every other position's output Tᵢ corresponds to its token and is used for token-level tasks like QA and tagging.

callout.title: The [CLS] vector isn't directly usable as sentence meaning
callout.text: Many people take a pretrained BERT and directly use the [CLS] output as the sentence's semantic vector for similarity. A paper footnote cautions: before fine-tuning, vector C is not a meaningful sentence representation, because during pretraining it was only used for NSP. To use it, first fine-tune on a specific task.

blocks.p: BERT's architecture is the original Transformer encoder; the paper says the implementation is "almost identical to the original," so it doesn't describe it exhaustively. The paper uses L for layers, H for hidden size, and A for attention heads; feed-forward width is always 4H. It reports two sizes:

fig.title: BERT's two sizes, compared with the other large models the paper mentions
fig.subtitle: From paper section 3 and section 5.2. The two amber rows are BERT.
rows: Largest Transformer in the literature cited by the paper
fig.note: BERT-BASE's feed-forward width is 3072; LARGE's is 4096.

blocks.p: BERT-BASE's size was **deliberately** chosen to match OpenAI GPT for a fair comparison. The paper stresses the two are nearly identical structurally; the key difference is one: BERT uses bidirectional self-attention, while GPT uses constrained self-attention where each token can see only its left context. The paper's footnote also explains a naming convention that later became standard: the bidirectional version is usually called a "Transformer encoder," and the left-only version a "Transformer decoder" because it can generate text.

sections.h: How pretraining works: 3.3 billion words, 4 days

list: **Data**: BooksCorpus (800M words) plus English Wikipedia (2.5B words). For Wikipedia, only text passages are used; lists, tables, and headers are ignored. The paper stresses using a document-level corpus rather than a shuffled sentence-level corpus, because it needs long contiguous sequences and next-sentence prediction requires real context.
**Scale**: 256 sequences per batch × 512 tokens = 128,000 tokens per batch, trained for 1,000,000 steps — about 40 passes over the 3.3-billion-word corpus.

**Optimization**: Adam, learning rate 1e-4, 10,000 warmup steps then linear decay; dropout 0.1 in all layers; GELU activation rather than ReLU (same as OpenAI GPT). The loss is the sum of the masked-LM loss and the next-sentence-prediction loss.
**Compute**: BASE uses 16 TPU chips and LARGE uses 64; each trains for 4 days.

blocks.p: There is also a detail that directly echoes our previous close reading: long sequences cost disproportionately more because attention computation grows quadratically with sequence length. So the authors use length-128 sequences for the first 90% of training steps and switch to length-512 only for the final 10%, mainly so the model learns the position embeddings for later positions. The n² problem from the Transformer paper is already shaping engineering decisions here.

quiz.q: If compute scales quadratically, roughly how much more attention computation does a length-512 sequence require than a length-128 sequence?
options: The same
quiz.why: The length increases 4× (512 ÷ 128), so the number of pairwise attention comparisons grows 4² = 16×. That is why the paper trains most steps on shorter sequences. Note this is only the attention part; feed-forward computation grows only linearly with length.

sections.h: Fine-tuning: add one layer and handle any task

blocks.p: After pretraining, using BERT on a task is straightforward: feed the task's input into BERT in the format above, attach a layer to the appropriate output, and retrain **all parameters** together on that task's labeled data. Each task starts from the same pretrained parameters and ends with its own fine-tuned model.

fig.title: Four task types, one BERT: inputs and outputs are all that change
fig.subtitle: Based on paper section 3.2 and appendix Figure 4.
rows: MNLI: infer whether the second sentence follows from the first
SST-2: positive or negative movie review
SQuAD: find the answer in the passage
Output Tᵢ for every passage token
Start vector S and end vector E
NER: identify person and place names

blocks.p: The classification formula is very short:

parts.desc: The final-layer output for [CLS], a vector of length H, representing the whole input
The only new parameter, shape K × H, where K is the number of classes (for example, an inference task has three: entailment, contradiction, neutral)
Turns K scores into K probabilities; training maximizes the log probability of the correct class

blocks.p: QA is slightly more complex, but the idea is just as elegant. Only two new vectors are added during fine-tuning: start vector S and end vector E. The dot product of each passage token's output Tᵢ with S is the score for "answer starts here":

formula.expr: P_{start}(i) = e^{S·T_i} / Σⱼ e^{S·T_j}   Candidate answer (i, j) score = S·T_i + E·T_j, with j ≥ i

parts.desc: The final-layer output at the i-th passage token
Two vectors learned during fine-tuning, scoring how much each position looks like a start or an end
The end position cannot come before the start; take the highest-scoring span as the answer

formula.note: The training objective maximizes the sum of the log probabilities of the correct start and end positions.

plain.title: One pen for the start, one for the end
plain.text: In QA, the answer is a contiguous span somewhere in the passage. BERT uses two vectors S and E to give every word two scores: how likely it is the start, and how likely it is the end. Pick the span with the highest "start + end" score whose end isn't before its start; that span is the answer (here, "soft mat").

fig.title: A worked example: finding the answer to "Where is the cat sitting?" in a passage
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: scores are invented, not paper data. Passage tokens: "cat / sits on / soft / mat / on / sleeping."
fig.note: The highest-scoring combination starts at "soft" and ends at "mat": 3.1 + 2.9 = 6.0, so the answer is "soft mat." Choosing an end before "soft" violates j ≥ i.

blocks.p: SQuAD 2.0 adds cases where the passage has no answer at all. BERT handles this just as simply: treat "no answer" as a special answer whose start and end both fall on [CLS], with score S·C + E·C. It outputs an answer only when the best real answer beats that score by a threshold τ, chosen on the dev set to maximize F1.

Fine-tuning cost is negligible compared with pretraining. The paper says all results start from the same pretrained model and can be replicated in at most 1 hour on one Cloud TPU, or a few hours on a GPU. For example, the SQuAD model reaches 91.0 dev F1 in about 30 minutes. All GLUE tasks use batch size 32 and 3 epochs. However, BERT-LARGE is occasionally unstable when fine-tuning on small datasets; the authors' approach is to run several random restarts and pick the best on the dev set.

quiz.q: When fine-tuning BERT-LARGE on SQuAD v1.1, how many new parameters are added beyond BERT's own parameters?
options: About 340M
2 × 1024 = 2048 (start vector S and end vector E)
30,000, one for each word in the vocabulary
quiz.why: The paper explicitly says SQuAD fine-tuning only introduces a start vector S and an end vector E, both of length equal to hidden size H. LARGE has H = 1024, so 2048 new parameters total; the other 340M parameters come from pretraining and are also updated during fine-tuning. This is what "one extra layer is all it takes" means.

sections.h: Report card: new records across 11 tasks

callout.title: What GLUE and SQuAD are
list: **GLUE**: a suite of nine language-understanding tasks, including sentence-relationship inference, sentiment, grammatical acceptability, and whether two sentences have the same meaning. The paper drops the problematic WNLI and reports the other eight.

**SQuAD**: Stanford's reading-comprehension dataset: given a Wikipedia passage and a question, mark the answer span in the passage. v1.1 has about 100,000 QA pairs; v2.0 adds questions with no answer in the passage.
**F1**: measures overlap between the predicted answer and the ground-truth answer, max 100; **EM** is exact match.

fig.title: Average GLUE score across eight tasks: BERT-BASE already beats GPT by 4.5 points
fig.subtitle: Units: points, GLUE test set, excluding WNLI. Amber is BERT; BERT-BASE and GPT have nearly identical architecture and the same size.
fig.note: From paper Table 1. The average here is computed differently from the official GLUE total score; on the official leaderboard, BERT-LARGE is 80.5 and GPT is 72.8.

fig.title: The less training data a task has, the bigger BERT's gain
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 1 (GLUE test set). Parentheses show number of training examples; blue bars are BERT-LARGE.
fig.note: For MNLI only the matched evaluation is listed. "Gain" is our subtraction from the paper's table.

blocks.p: On reading comprehension, the BERT-LARGE ensemble (fine-tuned first on TriviaQA, then on SQuAD) reaches 93.2 F1 on the SQuAD v1.1 test set, 1.5 points above the previous top ensemble system; a single model already beats the best ensemble. The paper adds that skipping TriviaQA costs only 0.1–0.4 F1. On SQuAD v2.0, a single BERT-LARGE reaches 83.1 F1, 5.1 points above the previous best system.

fig.title: Three reading and commonsense tasks: previous best and humans compared
fig.subtitle: Test sets, from paper Tables 2–4; human scores from leaderboards or dataset papers. Blue bars are BERT.

callout.title: “Beating humans” depends on what exactly is being compared
callout.text: On SQuAD v1.1, BERT’s F1 is higher than the human score in the table, but that “human score” is a leaderboard baseline computed from crowdsourced annotations, and in v1.1 the answer always appears in the passage. Switch to v2.0, which adds “no answer” questions, and BERT’s 83.1 is clearly below the human 89.5. One number beating a human baseline does not mean the model has surpassed human reading comprehension.

blocks.p: On SWAG — given a sentence, choose the most plausible continuation from four candidates — BERT-LARGE scores 27.1 points above the dataset authors’ baseline and 8.3 points above GPT.

sections.h: Ablations: where does the gain really come from?

blocks.p: Besides bidirectionality, BERT and GPT differ in several ways: BERT uses more data (GPT used only BooksCorpus), larger batches, and learns [SEP], [CLS], and segment embeddings during pretraining. The appendix candidly lists these differences and uses ablations to answer: where does the improvement really come from?

fig.title: Remove NSP, then make it unidirectional: QA drops hardest
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 5, dev set, all using BERT-BASE architecture and the same data. Blue bars are SQuAD.
rows: Then switch to left-to-right (≈ GPT’s approach)

blocks.p: Three things stand out. First, removing NSP clearly hurts QNLI, MNLI, and SQuAD. Second, switching from bidirectional to unidirectional (row 3, with the same data and fine-tuning setup, roughly GPT’s approach) hurts every task, with MRPC and SQuAD suffering most: SQuAD falls from 87.9 to 77.8. The paper’s explanation is intuitive: in a left-to-right model, every token’s representation lacks right-side information, and locating an answer’s position is exactly what needs the right side. Third, adding a bidirectional LSTM on top of the unidirectional model lifts SQuAD back to 84.9, still far below true bidirectional pretraining, and actually worsens GLUE tasks.

The paper also responds to the idea of training two unidirectional models and concatenating them, as ELMo does: it costs twice as much as one bidirectional model. It is unnatural for QA because a right-to-left model cannot condition its reading of the answer on the question, and it is strictly less powerful, because a deep bidirectional model can use both sides at **every layer**.

fig.title: Bigger is better, even for a task with only 3,600 training examples
fig.subtitle: Units: MNLI dev accuracy (average of 5 fine-tuning runs). From paper Table 6; amber rows are BERT-BASE and BERT-LARGE.
fig.note: The same table shows MRPC (only 3,600 training examples) climbing from 79.8 to 87.8.

blocks.p: The paper argues this is the first work to convincingly demonstrate that **scaling to very large models also yields large improvements on very small tasks**, provided the model is sufficiently pretrained. Earlier feature-based work was mixed on whether bigger models helped; the authors’ guess is that direct fine-tuning with very few new parameters lets downstream tasks fully benefit from larger, more expressive pretrained representations even when task data is scarce. The appendix adds that 1M pretraining steps beats 500k by almost 1 point on MNLI.

callout.title: Fine-tuning is not the only way to use it
callout.text: Paper section 5.3 also tests feature-based use: freeze BERT’s parameters, extract intermediate outputs as features, and feed them into a small model for named entity recognition. Concatenating the last four layers reaches dev F1 96.1, only 0.3 below fine-tuning the whole model (96.4). This is more compute-efficient when you need many experiments or when a task doesn’t fit neatly into a Transformer.

quiz.q: In Table 5, which change causes the largest drop in SQuAD? What does that show?
options: Removing NSP, showing NSP is the most important part of BERT
Switching from bidirectional to left-to-right, showing token-level tasks especially need right-side context
Adding a bidirectional LSTM, showing LSTMs are harmful
All three changes have the same effect
quiz.why: Removing NSP drops SQuAD from 88.5 to 87.9; changing from bidirectional to left-to-right on top of that drops it from 87.9 to 77.8, the largest drop in the table. QA needs to judge whether each position is the start or end of the answer, so every token needs to know what is on its right — exactly the value of bidirectionality.

sections.h: What it didn’t solve, and what came next

list: **Pretrain–fine-tune mismatch**: [MASK] appears only during pretraining; 80/10/10 is a mitigation, not a cure. It also predicts only 15% of tokens per batch, so training is less efficient.
**The value of next-sentence prediction is questionable**: as noted earlier, later work at larger scale found that dropping NSP does no harm.
**Length limit**: inputs are capped at 512 tokens, still driven by the quadratic cost of attention.

**Weak at generation**: BERT is an encoder—great at “reading” but with no natural word-by-word generation method. The paper’s own footnote notes that the left-only “decoder” is the one suited to generating text.
**Unstable fine-tuning on small datasets**: BERT-LARGE needs multiple random restarts to pick a good result on small datasets.

blocks.p: After BERT, “pretrain + fine-tune” quickly became standard practice in NLP, and improved variants proliferated. But the line leading to today’s large chat models went another way: the GPT lineage kept the left-to-right language model and kept scaling up model and data, so that by GPT-3 (2020) many tasks no longer needed fine-tuning at all—a few examples in the prompt sufficed. Those papers are all in our reading list, and we’ll cover them one by one.

callout.title: What to read next
callout.text: GPT-3’s “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners” covers doing tasks without fine-tuning; “Scaling Laws” covers how far the bigger-is-better pattern goes. Both are in the reading list.

sections.h: Test yourself: have you really understood it?

quiz.q: What is the most important architectural difference between BERT and GPT?
options: BERT uses LSTM; GPT uses Transformer
BERT’s self-attention can see both left and right; in GPT each token can see only the left
BERT has 10× more parameters than GPT
BERT does not need pretraining
quiz.why: The paper deliberately makes BERT-BASE the same size as GPT and stresses that the two architectures are nearly identical; the only difference is how attention is masked: BERT is bidirectional, GPT is left-only. That difference is also what forces BERT to use masked-word prediction.

callout.title: After reading, you should be able to answer these five questions in your own words.
list: Where do unidirectional language models fall short on language-understanding tasks? Give an example.
Why can’t a language model simply be made bidirectional? How does masked-word prediction get around this?
Why are the selected words treated three ways: 80%, 10%, 10%?
How is the same BERT used for three different tasks—classification, QA, and token-level tagging?
What do the ablations show about where BERT’s gains mainly come from?
